claim: A mouse in the labyrinth makes approximately 2000 navigation decisions per hour.
source: A mouse in the labyrinth makes ~2000 navigation decisions per hour.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a measured observation from the experiments.

claim: Mice execute correct 10-bit choices after only 10 reward experiences.
source: The animal explores the maze, quickly discovers the location of a reward, and executes correct 10-bit choices after only 10 reward experiences — a learning rate 1000-fold higher than in 2AFC experiments.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract summarizing experimental findings, with the 1000-fold comparison providing context.

claim: The learning rate in the labyrinth is 1000-fold higher than in 2AFC experiments.
source: The animal explores the maze, quickly discovers the location of a reward, and executes correct 10-bit choices after only 10 reward experiences — a learning rate 1000-fold higher than in 2AFC experiments.
evidence: This comparison is explicitly stated in the abstract, based on the observed learning rate in the labyrinth versus reported rates in 2AFC tasks.

claim: Many mice improve discontinuously from one minute to the next, suggesting moments of sudden insight.
source: Many mice improve discontinuously from one minute to the next, suggesting moments of sudden insight about the structure of the labyrinth.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data analysis in Figure 5 showing sudden changes in behavior.

claim: The underlying search algorithm does not require a global memory of places visited.
source: The underlying search algorithm does not require a global memory of places visited and is largely explained by purely local turning rules.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by analysis of turning biases in Figure 9.

claim: The search algorithm is largely explained by purely local turning rules.
source: The underlying search algorithm does not require a global memory of places visited and is largely explained by purely local turning rules.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through biased random walk models in Figure 9.

claim: The Bruce effect is an instance of one-shot learning in mice.
source: In laboratory studies, one prominent instance of one-shot learning is the Bruce effect (Bruce, 1959).
evidence: This is stated directly with a citation to Bruce, 1959.

claim: In the Bruce effect, the female mouse forms an olfactory memory of her mating partner that allows her to terminate the pregnancy if she encounters another male that threatens infanticide.
source: Here, the female mouse forms an olfactory memory of her mating partner that allows her to terminate the pregnancy if she encounters another male that threatens infanticide.
evidence: This describes the Bruce effect mechanism with reference to the cited work.

claim: Fear conditioning is a form of rapid learning accessible to laboratory experiments.
source: Another form of rapid learning accessible to laboratory experiments is fear conditioning, where a formerly innocuous stimulus gets associated with a painful experience, leading to subsequent avoidance of the stimulus (Fanselow and Bolles, 1979; Bourtchuladze et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: A mouse typically requires many weeks of shaping and thousands of trials to reach asymptotic performance in 2AFC tasks.
source: Remarkably, they are learned exceedingly slowly: a mouse typically requires many weeks of shaping and thousands of trials to reach asymptotic performance; a monkey may require many months (Carandini and Churchland, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Carandini and Churchland, 2013.

claim: A monkey may require many months to learn 2AFC tasks.
source: Remarkably, they are learned exceedingly slowly: a mouse typically requires many weeks of shaping and thousands of trials to reach asymptotic performance; a monkey may require many months (Carandini and Churchland, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Carandini and Churchland, 2013.

claim: The maze is structured as a binary tree with 63 branch points and 64 end nodes.
source: The maze is structured as a binary tree with 63 branch points (in levels numbered 0,…,5) and 64 end nodes.
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption for Figure 1 and shown in the figure.

claim: One end node has a water port that dispenses a drop when it gets poked.
source: One end node has a water port that dispenses a drop when it gets poked.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1 caption and shown in the figure.

claim: All the mice except one passed between the cage and the maze readily and frequently.
source: All the mice except one passed between the cage and the maze readily and frequently (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: One mouse barely entered the maze and never progressed past the first junction and was excluded from analysis.
source: The single outlier animal barely entered the maze and never progressed past the first junction; we excluded this mouse's data from subsequent analysis.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text describing the experimental results.

claim: On average over the entire period of study the animals spent 46% of the time in the maze.
source: On average over the entire period of study the animals spent 46% of the time in the maze (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to supporting figure data.

claim: The fraction of time spent in the maze was similar whether or not the animal was motivated by water rewards (47% for rewarded vs 44% for unrewarded animals).
source: This fraction was similar whether or not the animal was motivated by water rewards (47% for rewarded vs 44% for unrewarded animals).
evidence: This comparison is stated directly based on experimental data.

claim: The rate of entry into the maze is highest immediately after the animal returns to the cage.
source: Surprisingly the rate of entry into the maze is highest immediately after the animal returns to the cage.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The rate of entry into the maze declines gradually by a factor of 4 over the first minute in the cage and remains steady thereafter.
source: Then it declines gradually by a factor of 4 over the first minute in the cage and remains steady thereafter.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the analysis of transition rates.

claim: The exit from the maze occurs at an essentially constant rate throughout the visit.
source: By contrast the opposite transition, namely exit from the maze, occurs at an essentially constant rate throughout the visit (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to supporting figure.

claim: All 10 water-deprived animals discovered the water port in less than 2000 s and fewer than 17 bouts.
source: Yet, all 10 discovered the water port in less than 2000 s and fewer than 17 bouts (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 3A showing the timeline of rewards.

claim: Late in the night approximately 75% of the paths to water were perfect.
source: Late in the night ~75% of the paths to water were perfect.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the learning curve results.

claim: Fast water runs took as little as 2 s.
source: The animals executed them with increasing speed; eventually, these fast 'water runs' took as little as 2 s (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 3B showing run durations.

claim: Three of the four animals went to the correct water port on their first entry into the maze immediately after rotation, before ever visiting the image location.
source: Immediately after rotation, three of the four animals went to the correct water port on their first entry into the maze, and before ever visiting the image location (e.g. Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the maze rotation experiment results.

claim: The fourth mouse visited the image location once and then the correct water port after maze rotation.
source: The fourth mouse visited the image location once and then the correct water port (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to supporting figure.

claim: Visits to the image location increased by a factor of 1.8 after maze rotation.
source: Visits to the image location were at chance levels prior to rotation, then increased by a factor of 1.8.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the effects of maze rotation.

claim: Visits to the water port declined in frequency after rotation, although they still exceeded visits to the image location by a factor of 5.
source: Visits to the water port declined in frequency, although they still exceeded visits to the image location by a factor of 5.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the maze rotation results.

claim: The reward rate declined by a factor of 0.7 after maze rotation.
source: The reward rate declined by a factor of 0.7.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the effects of maze rotation.

claim: For navigation to the water port, experienced animals do not strictly depend on physical cues that are attached to the maze.
source: In summary, for navigation to the water port the experienced animals do not strictly depend on physical cues that are attached to the maze.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the maze rotation experiment results.

claim: At least 5 of the 10 water-deprived animals showed discontinuities in behavior that could be identified to a precision of approximately 200 s.
source: Similar discontinuities in behavior were seen in at least 5 of the 10 water-deprived animals (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—source data 1), and their timing could be identified to a precision of ~200 s.
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to supporting figures and data.

claim: With few exceptions, the first home run began from an end node, as deep into the maze as possible.
source: With few exceptions, that first home run began from an end node, as deep into the maze as possible.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 6A results.

claim: The end nodes (level 7 of the maze) are by far the favorite place from which to return to the exit.
source: In fact, the end nodes (level 7 of the maze) are by far the favorite place from which to return to the exit, and those maximal-length home runs systematically appear before shorter ones.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 6B results.

claim: The entry path and the home path tend to have little overlap.
source: Instead the entry path and the home path tend to have little overlap (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 6C showing overlap distributions.

claim: The minimum overlap between entry and home paths is 1, because all paths into and out of the maze have to pass through the central junction.
source: Note the minimum overlap is 1, because all paths into and out of the maze have to pass through the central junction (node 0 in Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text explaining the overlap analysis.

claim: The animals spent most of their time by far in the exploration state: 84% for rewarded and 95% for unrewarded mice.
source: The animals spent most of their time by far in the exploration state: 84% for rewarded and 95% for unrewarded mice.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the behavioral state analysis.

claim: The rewarded mice began about half their bouts into the maze with a trip to the water port and the other half by exploring.
source: The rewarded mice began about half their bouts into the maze with a trip to the water port and the other half by exploring (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 7A showing the ethogram.

claim: After a drink, the animals routinely continued exploring, about 90% of the time.
source: After a drink, the animals routinely continued exploring, about 90% of the time.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing behavioral transitions.

claim: The efficiency of exploration varied by only 11% of the mean (0.387 ± 0.044 SD) across animals.
source: The different mice were remarkably alike in this component of their exploratory behavior (Figure 8B): across animals the efficiency varied by only 11% of the mean (0.387 ± 0.044 SD).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 8B showing exploration efficiency.

claim: There was no detectable difference in exploration efficiency between the rewarded animals and the sated unrewarded animals.
source: Furthermore, there was no detectable difference in efficiency between the rewarded animals and the sated unrewarded animals.
evidence: This is stated in the text comparing the two groups.

claim: Over the course of the night, the exploration efficiency declined significantly for almost every animal by an average of 23%.
source: Over the course of the night, the efficiency declined significantly for almost every animal – whether rewarded or not – by an average of 23% (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 8C showing the decline.

claim: The turning biases varied by only 3% across the population and even between the rewarded and unrewarded groups.
source: A comparison across animals again revealed a remarkable degree of consistency even in these local rules of behavior: The turning biases varied by only 3% across the population and even between the rewarded and unrewarded groups (Figure 9B, Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 9B and source data.

claim: Biased random agents search with much higher efficiency than the unbiased random walk.
source: These biased agents did in fact search with much higher efficiency than the unbiased random walk.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing simulation results.

claim: Biased agents accounted for approximately 87% of the animal's efficiency (compared to 60% for the random walk).
source: They did not fully explain the behavior of the mice (Figure 9D), accounting for ~87% of the animal's efficiency (compared to 60% for the random walk).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 9D.

claim: Animals visit certain end nodes of the binary tree much more frequently than others, with more than a factor of 10 difference between the most popular and least popular end nodes.
source: A surprising aspect of the animals' explorations is that they visit certain end nodes of the binary tree much more frequently than others (Figure 10). This effect is large: more than a factor of 10 difference between the occupancy of the most popular and least popular end nodes (Figure 10A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 10 showing node preferences.

claim: The node preferences were very consistent across animals and even across the rewarded and unrewarded groups.
source: Furthermore, the node preferences were very consistent across animals and even across the rewarded and unrewarded groups.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the node preference analysis.

claim: The nodes on the periphery of the maze are systematically preferred, with the outermost ring favored by a large factor of 2.2 compared to the innermost nodes.
source: The nodes on the periphery of the maze are systematically preferred. Comparing the outermost ring of 26 end nodes (excluding the water port and its neighbor) to the innermost 16 end nodes, the outer ones are favored by a large factor of 2.2.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing spatial preferences in exploration.

claim: The biased random walk using four bias numbers predicts 51% of the observed variance across nodes for unrewarded animals.
source: For unrewarded animals, where the maze symmetry is not disturbed by the water port, the biased random walk predicts 51% of the observed variance across nodes (Figure 10C), and an outer/inner node preference of 1.97, almost matching the observed ratio of 2.20.
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 10C showing the comparison.

claim: The remaining uncertainty about the animal's action at a T-junction is 1.237 ± 0.035 (SD) bits/action across all 19 animals.
source: Across all 19 animals in this study the remaining uncertainty about the animal's action at a T-junction is 1.237 ± 0.035 (SD) bits/action, compared to the prior uncertainty of log2 3 = 1.585 bits.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the Markov model results.

claim: The rewarded animals have slightly lower entropy than the unrewarded ones (1.216 vs 1.261 bits/action).
source: The rewarded animals have slightly lower entropy than the unrewarded ones (1.216 vs 1.261 bits/action).
evidence: This comparison is stated directly in the text.

claim: The Markov chain models that produced the best fits to the behavior used history strings with an average length of approximately 4.
source: The Markov chain models that produced the best fits to the behavior used history strings with an average length of ~4.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the model fitting results.

claim: The median mouse performed 16,192 steps in the 7 h period of observation (mean = 15,257; SD = 3340).
source: The median mouse performed 16,192 steps in the 7 h period of observation (mean = 15,257; SD = 3340).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the reduced trajectories.

claim: The maze measured approximately 24 x 24 x 2 inches.
source: The maze measured ~24 x 24 x 2 inches; for manufacture we used materials specified in inches, so dimensions are quoted in those non-SI units where appropriate.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing maze construction.

claim: The resulting corridors were 1-1/8 inches wide.
source: The resulting corridors (1-1/8 inches wide) formed a 6-level binary tree with T-junctions and progressive shortening of each branch, ranging from ~12 inch to 1.5 inch (Figure 1 and Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing maze construction.

claim: The water reward port delivered approximately 30 µL of water per reward.
source: The interface briefly opened the water valve to deliver ~30 µL of water and flashed an infrared LED mounted outside the maze for 1 s.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the reward delivery system.

claim: Following each reward, the system entered a time-out period for 90 s.
source: Following each reward, the system entered a time-out period for 90 s, during which the port did not provide further reward.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the reward delivery system.

claim: All mice were C57BL/6J animals between the ages of 45 and 98 days (mean 62 days).
source: All mice were C57BL/6J animals (Jackson Labs) between the ages of 45 and 98 days (mean 62 days).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing animals and treatments.

claim: Four males and six females were used in the rewarded experiments, and five males and four females in the unrewarded experiments.
source: Both sexes were used: four males and six females in the rewarded experiments, five males and four females in the unrewarded experiments.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing animals and treatments.

claim: For water deprivation, the animal was transferred from its home cage to the maze cage approximately 22 h before the start of the experiment.
source: For water deprivation, the animal was transferred from its home cage (generally group-housed) to the maze cage ~22 h before the start of the experiment.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing animals and treatments.

claim: The learning rate in the labyrinth is approximately 10 bits/h compared to less than 1 bit/month in 2AFC tasks, a difference of a factor of 6000.
source: The rate of learning, measured in task complexity per unit time, is surprisingly low: less than 1 bit/month compared to ~10 bits/h observed in the labyrinth. The difference is a factor of 6000.
evidence: This comparison is stated in the Discussion section based on the experimental results and literature comparison.

claim: The 2AFC mouse may need 5000 rewards to learn a contingency table with one bit complexity, whereas the mouse in the maze needs approximately 10 rewards to learn 10 bits.
source: Similarly when measured in complexity learned per reward experience: The 2AFC mouse may need 5000 rewards to learn a contingency table with one bit complexity, whereas the mouse in the maze needs ~10 rewards to learn 10 bits.
evidence: This comparison is stated in the Discussion section based on experimental results and literature.

claim: Bees will extend their proboscis in response to a new odor after just one pairing trial where the odor appeared together with sugar.
source: For example, bees will extend their proboscis in response to a new odor after just one pairing trial where the odor appeared together with sugar (Bitterman et al., 1983).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Bitterman et al., 1983.

claim: Rodents will start digging for food in a scented bowl after just a few pairings with that odor.
source: Similarly, rodents will start digging for food in a scented bowl after just a few pairings with that odor (Cleland et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Cleland et al., 2009.

claim: The path from the maze entrance to the water port involves six junctions, each with three options, which involves 6·log2 3 = 9.5 bits of complexity.
source: For example, the path from the maze entrance to the water port involves six junctions, each with three options. At a minimum six different contexts must be mapped correctly into one of three actions each, which involves 6·log23 = 9.5 bits of complexity.
evidence: This calculation is stated in the Discussion section based on the maze structure.

claim: If the animal could turn correctly towards water from each of 63 junctions in the maze, it would have learned 63·log2 3 = 100 bits.
source: In the limit, if the animal could turn correctly towards water from each of 63 junctions in the maze, it would have learned 63·log23 = 100 bits.
evidence: This calculation is stated in the Discussion section as a theoretical limit.

claim: The animals have mastered 10–20 bits of complexity based on 10–20 reward experiences within an hour of time spent in the maze.
source: Conservatively, we estimate that the animals have mastered 10–20 bits of complexity based on 10–20 reward experiences within an hour of time spent in the maze.
evidence: This estimate is stated in the Discussion section based on the experimental results.

claim: Approximately 10 successful trials are sufficient for rats to learn approximately 10 decisions in diverse mazes and problem boxes.
source: Although those tasks come in many varieties, a common theme is that ~10 successful trials are sufficient to learn ~10 decisions (Woodrow, 1942).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Woodrow, 1942.

claim: The mouse with the steering wheel in 2AFC tasks requires about 10,000 experiences before performance saturates.
source: For example, the mouse with the steering wheel requires about 10,000 experiences before performance saturates.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section comparing learning rates.

claim: The typical hit rate in 2AFC tasks is only 2/3 of the way from random to perfect.
source: It never gets particularly good, with a typical hit rate only 2/3 of the way from random to perfect.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing 2AFC performance.

claim: The 2AFC training takes 3–6 weeks for mice and several months for monkeys.
source: All this training takes 3–6 weeks; in the case of monkeys several months.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section comparing learning rates.

claim: The rotation image of the water port is one of the most popular destinations for rewarded animals.
source: Finally, a partial clue comes from errors the animals make. We found that the rotation image of the water port, an end node diametrically across the entire maze, is one of the most popular destinations for rewarded animals (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to Figure 10A.

claim: If the animal navigated via a remembered sequence of turns, then it will end up at the image node if it makes a single mistake at just the first T-junction.
source: On the other hand, if the animal navigates via a remembered sequence of turns, then it will end up at that image node if it makes a single mistake at just the first T-junction.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference about navigation mechanisms.

claim: The speed of locomotion is approximately constant at ~1.56 cells/s = 5.94 cm/s on average.
source: Note that the speed is very similar across animals, ~1.56 cells/s = 5.94 cm/s on average.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The speed rises quickly over the first 50 s in the maze, then varies only little over the 7 h of the experiment.
source: It rises quickly over the first 50 s in the maze, then varies only little over the 7 h of the experiment.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Every time the mouse turns away from the shortest path to the water port that adds two steps to the path length.
source: Note the path length plotted here is directly related to the number of 'turning errors': every time the mouse turns away from the shortest path to the water port that adds two steps to the path length (Equation 7).
evidence: This relationship is stated in the text explaining the path length analysis.

claim: The maze rotation occurred after at least 6 h of exposure, by which time the animals had all perfected the direct path to the water port.
source: The maze rotation occurred after at least 6 h of exposure, by which time the animals had all perfected the direct path to the water port.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the maze rotation experiment.

claim: For animals 'D7' and 'D9' only the floor of the maze was rotated, leaving the walls and ceiling in the original configuration.
source: For animals 'D7' and 'D9' we rotated only the floor of the maze, leaving the walls and ceiling in the original configuration.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the maze rotation experiment.

claim: For 'F2' and 'A1' the entire maze was rotated, moving one wall segment at the central junction and the water port to attain the same shape.
source: For 'F2' and 'A1' we rotated the entire maze, moving one wall segment at the central junction and the water port to attain the same shape.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the maze rotation experiment.

claim: Navigation remained intact for all animals after maze rotation.
source: Navigation remained intact for all animals.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the maze rotation results.

claim: The biased random walk predicts an outer/inner node preference of 1.97, almost matching the observed ratio of 2.20.
source: For unrewarded animals, where the maze symmetry is not disturbed by the water port, the biased random walk predicts 51% of the observed variance across nodes (Figure 10C), and an outer/inner node preference of 1.97, almost matching the observed ratio of 2.20.
evidence: This comparison is stated in the text with reference to Figure 10C.

claim: The more complex Markov-chain model performed slightly better than the biased random walk, explaining 66% of the variance in port visits.
source: The more complex Markov-chain model of behavior (Figure 11C) performed slightly better, explaining 66% of the variance in port visits and matching the outer/inner node preference of 2.20.
evidence: This is stated in the text comparing model performance.

claim: The biased random walk using four bias numbers accounts for approximately 87% of the animal's efficiency but does not fully explain the behavior of the mice.
source: These biased agents did in fact search with much higher efficiency than the unbiased random walk. They did not fully explain the behavior of the mice (Figure 9D), accounting for ~87% of the animal's efficiency (compared to 60% for the random walk).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 9D.

claim: A more sophisticated Markov-chain model involving many more parameters failed to get any closer to the observed efficiency than the biased random walk.
source: A more sophisticated model of the animal's behavior - involving many more parameters (Figure 11C) - failed to get any closer to the observed efficiency (Figure 9C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text comparing model performance.

claim: The best file compression algorithm (bzip2) far under-performed all the other models of mouse behavior, giving 43% higher cross-entropy on average.
source: The best such algorithm (bzip2 compression Seward, 2019) far under-performed all the other models of mouse behavior, giving 43% higher cross-entropy on average, and thus offered no additional useful bounds.
evidence: This is stated in the text comparing different prediction methods.

claim: During exploration of the maze, the mouse's choice behavior is strongly influenced by its current location and approximately 3 locations preceding it.
source: We conclude that during exploration of the maze the mouse's choice behavior is strongly influenced by its current location and ~3 locations preceding it.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the Markov model analysis.

claim: By knowing the animal's history one can narrow down its action plan at a junction from the a priori 1.59 bits to just approximately 1.24 bits.
source: By knowing the animal's history one can narrow down its action plan at a junction from the a priori 1.59 bits (one of three possible actions) to just ~1.24 bits.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the Markov model analysis.

claim: The Bruce effect learning systems appear designed for special purposes and are likely implemented by specialized brain circuits.
source: These learning systems appear designed for special purposes, they perform very specific associations, and govern binary behavioral decisions. They are likely implemented by specialized brain circuits, and indeed great progress has been made in localizing these operations to the accessory olfactory bulb (Brennan and Keverne, 1997) and the cortical amygdala (LeDoux, 2000).
evidence: This is stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: The animal appears to acquire a homing strategy over the course of a single bout, in a manner that allows a direct return home even from locations not previously encountered.
source: In summary, it appears that the animal acquires a homing strategy over the course of a single bout, and in a manner that allows a direct return home even from locations not previously encountered.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the analysis of home runs in Figure 6.

claim: The animals do not practice the home path or build it up gradually.
source: Clearly, the animals do not practice the home path or build it up gradually.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the analysis showing maximal-length home runs appear first.

claim: The mouse does not follow the strategy of Theseus, namely to precisely retrace the path that led it into the labyrinth.
source: On the other hand, the mouse does not follow the strategy of Theseus, namely to precisely retrace the path that led it into the labyrinth.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the low overlap between entry and home paths.

claim: The animals seem to possess an Ariadne's thread starting with their first excursion into the maze, long before they might have acquired any general knowledge of the maze layout.
source: Clearly, the animals do not practice the home path or build it up gradually. Instead they seem to possess an Ariadne's thread (Apollodorus, 1921) starting with their first excursion into the maze, long before they might have acquired any general knowledge of the maze layout.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the home run data with a classical reference.

claim: One suspects that the animals derive some intrinsic reward from the act of patrolling the environment itself.
source: One suspects that the animals derive some intrinsic reward from the act of patrolling the environment itself.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the persistent exploration behavior.

claim: The animals seem to be governed by a set of local turning biases that require memory only of the most recent decision and no knowledge of location.
source: However, we found that a global long-term memory is not needed to explain the efficient search. The animals seem to be governed by a set of local turning biases that require memory only of the most recent decision and no knowledge of location (Figure 9).
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the analysis of turning biases.

claim: The local turning biases alone can explain most of the character of exploration without any global understanding or long-term memory.
source: These local biases alone can explain most of the character of exploration without any global understanding or long-term memory.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the biased random walk model results.

claim: The four decision probabilities for turning biases were identical across individuals to within a standard deviation of less than 0.03.
source: The four decision probabilities were identical across individuals to within a standard deviation of less than 0.03.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing the consistency of turning biases.

claim: It is possible that the rules for using tunnels are innate and determined genetically.
source: Given that tunnel systems are part of the mouse's natural ecology, it is possible that those rules are innate and determined genetically.
evidence: This is stated as speculation in the Discussion section.

claim: The rules by which mice build tunnels have a strong genetic component.
source: Indeed the rules by which mice build tunnels have a strong genetic component (Weber et al., 2013), so the rules for using tunnels may be written in the genes as well.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Weber et al., 2013.

claim: The discontinuous changes in performance pose a challenge to conventional models of reinforcement learning.
source: The discontinuous changes in performance pose a challenge to conventional models of reinforcement learning, in which reward events are the primary driver of learning and each event contributes an infinitesimal update to the action policy.
evidence: This is stated as an implication of the sudden insight findings.

claim: In conventional reinforcement learning models, reward events are the primary driver of learning and each event contributes an infinitesimal update to the action policy.
source: The discontinuous changes in performance pose a challenge to conventional models of reinforcement learning, in which reward events are the primary driver of learning and each event contributes an infinitesimal update to the action policy.
evidence: This characterizes conventional reinforcement learning as context for the challenge posed by the findings.

claim: The animal is most likely to enter the maze within the first minute of its return to the cage, a strong trend that runs opposite to the prediction from satiation of curiosity.
source: The animal is most likely to enter the maze within the first minute of its return to the cage (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), a strong trend that runs opposite to the prediction from satiation of curiosity.
evidence: This is stated as an observation that contradicts the homeostatic drive hypothesis.

claim: The drive to explore persists in 2AFC choice boxes, manifesting as an unexpectedly high error rate on unambiguous stimuli, sometimes called the 'lapse rate'.
source: Presumably the drive to explore persists, perhaps more so because the forced environment is so unpleasant. And within the confines of the two alternatives, the only act of exploration the mouse has left is to give the wrong answer. This would manifest as an unexpectedly high error rate on unambiguous stimuli, sometimes called the 'lapse rate' (Carandini and Churchland, 2013; Pisupati et al., 2021).
